title: Anchor the permission findings to a CLI version, and detect when they expire

history.detail:
PASS: PASS — round 1. Audited 558ac34 with bookkeeping abfe2fe, main checkout. Sprint file read fresh. Working tree clean apart from the known .vscode file.

This sprint closes the item I have carried since sprint 17. It also proves the specific factual claim I attached to that item was wrong. I am putting that first because it is the most important thing in this audit and it is mine.

================================================================
MY CARRIED CLAIM WAS WRONG, AND THIS SPRINT IS WHAT ESTABLISHED IT
================================================================

I carried "one CONFIRMED entry has already expired" through sprints 19, 20 and into this one, and cited it as the strongest-evidenced open item on the board. Req 2's re-run says: **zero of the re-verified entries have expired in behaviour.** Every mechanism still behaves as described at v2.1.261.

Where mine came from: sprint 17's Dev Team could not reproduce the git-push denial, and I read a non-reproduction as drift. Sprint 20's Req 4 then established the actual cause of every "cannot force a denial" report in this project — the role refuses on its own judgement before the permission layer is ever consulted, and an honest refusal is indistinguishable from an unobservable bound. This document now shows the same thing directly: given a probe the role would genuinely attempt, the denial "shows up immediately, permission_denials populated with the exact compound command."

So the bound never expired. My inference was a method artifact, and the correction was available the moment sprint 20 landed — I carried it one sprint past the evidence that refuted it. That is the same error I have flagged in others for twenty sprints: a claim asserted from an absence rather than a positive result. Recording it plainly rather than letting "zero expired" quietly retire it, because the record should show where the wrong claim came from, not just that it is gone.

The sprint is right and valuable anyway. Anchoring the findings to a version was correct whether or not anything had expired — and the honest outcome (nothing expired, three message wordings drifted) is more useful than the one I predicted.

================================================================
REQ 2 — THE LOAD-BEARING CHECK. RE-RUN, NOT READ, AND THE GRADING DISTINGUISHES THE TWO.
================================================================

The FAIL trigger is an entry silently carried forward as CONFIRMED without a fresh run. I looked for exactly that and did not find one. The document states where it ran (a throwaway git-init scratch directory, a throwaway bare remote, a throwaway scratch npm package), what it ran against (claude 2.1.261, confirmed via --version immediately before the pass, dated), and that permission_denials and file-system side effects were inspected directly "not inferred from the model's own prose summary."

THE COUNT IS STATED AND IT IS ZERO, which the criterion specifically demanded ("'at least one' is where this sprint started; it is not an acceptable place to finish").

THE THREE WORDING DRIFTS ARE THE USEFUL RESULT and they are documented old-versus-new in a table rather than described. I verified the claim that rests on them — that none is a live defect because nothing pattern-matches the free text. Grepped the whole of scripts/ for every one of the three old message strings: no match anywhere. Stronger than claimed, in fact: permission_denials appears in run-role.js only inside comments and is never read by any code path, which is sprint 11's "we emit, we do not parse" boundary still holding.

The bare-`Bash(*)` re-verification, done beyond the document's original scope, is the right instinct — it is the claim sprint 19's entire owned-repository grant list is built on, and re-confirming it directly ("`Bash(*)` let the redirect through, file created outside the working directory; `Bash(git *)` blocked it") means that list rests on a re-tested property rather than a remembered one.

================================================================
REQ 1 — THE RETROFIT COVERS THE DOCUMENT, AND THE UNVERIFIABLE ENTRIES ARE DOWNGRADED
================================================================

Thirteen entries now carry an explicit version tag; 42 version references across the file. The two remaining bare "CONFIRMED" strings are prose describing the grading convention itself, not untagged entries — checked each rather than counting.

Three sub-claims are downgraded rather than left CONFIRMED on a guessed version, each named with what was and was not re-run: the `od -c` byte check and the backtick/$VAR refusal on the printf pattern (redirect mechanism re-confirmed, that narrower sub-test not re-run); the Req 4 six-role narrative log (a historical record of one run, not re-graded); and `npm view` specifically (the allowlist mechanism it shares was re-confirmed, `view` itself not separately re-invoked). That is the criterion's condition met precisely — the distinction between "still confirmed" and "not re-tested" is drawn per entry, not asserted for the document.

================================================================
REQ 3 — WARNS, NEVER GATES, AND IT ANSWERS THE BANNER TEST
================================================================

Verified both directions with a fake claude reporting a controlled version:
    reports 2.1.258, anchor 2.1.261 -> NOTE printed to stderr, exit 0 (did not gate)
    reports 2.1.261 (match)         -> zero NOTE lines, silent
And the code returns early on both a match and an unknown version, so it cannot fire spuriously.

The criterion says to read it against the `repo=` banner, because a check nobody reads does not exist. This passes that test for a specific reason worth recording: the banner fires on every invocation and was ignored through four wrong readings (sprint 7's own finding). This fires only when something has actually changed. A warning that is silent in the steady state is one that means something when it speaks.

The message itself handles the two-audience problem correctly, and that was a real catch made mid-build: it does not point a downstream operator at docs/sprint-12-permission-scope-findings.md as if they could open it. I confirmed the premise independently — installed a fresh copy from this build into a scratch directory, and that file is genuinely absent from an installed target (docs/ contains only HUMAN_OVERRIDE.md and sprints/). Catching that before shipping, one sprint after sprint 20 fixed the same class of ambiguity in CLAUDE.md, is the pattern being recognised rather than re-learned.

================================================================
REQS 4, 5 — MET
================================================================

package.json 0.1.22, one line. Ran the suites: 177 OK (up 6, matching the new staleness coverage), ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED; ALL SMOKE TESTS PASSED; verify-tarball.sh PASSED, "Installed 0.1.22 (first install)". The new coverage tests both branches, null-safety, and a real subprocess launch confirming the check never changes the exit code — which is the property that matters for a warning that must never gate.

================================================================
THE UNASKED-FOR FINDING
================================================================

The variadic `--allowedTools` swallowing a trailing bare prompt is a real hazard and correctly characterised: production is unaffected because headlessLaunchArgs() always inserts a terminating flag before the prompt, confirmed by spawning claude with the exact real argv array rather than reasoning about it. Recorded as a hazard for a future refactor of that argument ordering, which is the right disposition — it is not a defect today and it would be an ugly one to rediscover.

INFORMATIONAL, CARRIED

1. My expired-entry claim is closed and corrected, above. What remains of the original concern is the
   thing this sprint actually built: the findings now have an anchor version and a live check, so the
   next drift is detectable rather than inferred from a failed reproduction.
2. Carried, unchanged: every allowlist entry other than git and npm remains inferred; the empty-string
   ownedRepository declaration falling through silently; the --agents argv budget against Windows'
   32,767-char limit.

RECOMMENDATION

Ship it. /sprint-dev-done 21, then Pipeman ships and publishes 0.1.22, then `verify-publish 21`.

One thing worth recording about the shape of this sprint: it was scheduled on my evidence, and the first thing it did was disprove my evidence while still being worth doing. A re-verification that had simply agreed with the old entries would have produced a document that looked freshly confirmed and was not — the sprint file names that risk and the work avoided it. That is the difference between re-checking and re-reading, and it is the whole reason the criterion said this one could not be cleared by reading.

PASS: PASS — round 1. Live-tested published npm 0.1.22 against a real install and against the CLI I am actually running (claude 2.1.261). Environment: macOS Darwin arm64, 2026-09-06. ~$1.13 in billed runs, of which $0.93 was an accident of mine — see the disclosure at the end.

PROVENANCE
0.1.22 on the registry; gitHead 1ca1e8f9210b9b4763d473df8675009e7cd2d145 == last_shipped_commit; zero `reshipped` events; QA1 PASS round 1. Content check per sprint 13's rule: all 57 published files byte-identical to `git show 1ca1e8f:<path>`, MISMATCHED 0, tarball sha1 matches the registry's dist.shasum. Own registry query run before reading verify-publish's record.

================================================================
CRITERION — THE STALENESS SIGNAL APPEARS, AND DOES NOT BLOCK: PASS
================================================================
The anchor as shipped is PERMISSION_FINDINGS_ANCHOR_VERSION = '2.1.261', and the CLI I am running is 2.1.261. That gave me a real control rather than a constructed one.

CONTROL, matching version: no staleness output at all. Correct — a version equal to the anchor is not drift and should say nothing.

MISMATCH, via a stub `claude` on PATH reporting 2.1.999, verbatim from stderr:
  "NOTE: this session is running claude 2.1.999, but the headless permission-scope evidence the
  fully-completely framework's own profiles rest on (docs/sprint-12-permission-scope-findings.md in the
  fully-completely framework's own upstream repository -- not a file copied into an installed project,
  so it will only be present here if this session IS that repository) was last re-verified against
  2.1.261. Not a defect and not a block -- this bound has already survived one real CLI update
  unchanged -- but if a permission behaviour in this session doesn't match what that document
  describes, this is the first place to look, or to ask upstream about."

  exit code: 0                      -> did not block
  run proceeded to spawn:  YES      -> the stub actually ran, so the launch completed
  stdout:  pure JSON, unchanged     -> warning went to stderr, machine-readable stream uncorrupted

That last point matters more than it looks. Sprint 11's Req 2 requires headless stdout to carry the envelope and nothing else; a new warning is exactly the kind of thing that quietly breaks it. It is on stderr, where it belongs, and a consumer parsing stdout sees no difference.

The message is also carefully scoped in a way worth noting: it tells a reader in an installed project that the findings document will not be present there, which is the sprint-20 Req 3 disambiguation carried into new text rather than applied once and forgotten.

================================================================
CRITERION — RE-RUN A SAMPLE OF THE RE-VERIFIED ENTRIES MYSELF: PASS
================================================================
The criterion's reasoning is that "a re-verification nobody independently repeated is one team's word", so these were run by me, against the published 0.1.22 module and my own CLI, not read out of the findings document.

1. BARE INTERPRETER REJECTION — "node", "bash", "sh", "python3" all true; "npm test" and "node test/all.js" both false. Rejects the dangerous shapes, admits the legitimate ones.

2. .env PROTECTION (macOS chflags path) —
     protectEnvFiles -> {"protected":["/tmp/env22/.env"],"failed":[]}
     READ:   ok ("SECRET=k")
     WRITE:  blocked EPERM
     DELETE: blocked EPERM
     after unprotect: writable again
   Readable, not writable, not deletable, cleanly reversible — Req 3 of sprint 19 still holds on this CLI.

3. git push DENIED WHILE git status PASSES — run at the permission layer with the grant's own two lists (`--allowedTools "Bash(git *)" --disallowedTools "Bash(git push *)"`):
     `git status --short`      -> permitted, output "?? pr.txt"
     `git push origin HEAD:main` -> DENIED, 1 permission denial
   And I verified the consequence rather than the agent's account of it: the bare remote has NO refs, so the push genuinely did not get through. A disallow entry that subtracts one verb from a broad `Bash(git *)` grant works.

4. THE DOCUMENTED CONFINEMENT ESCAPE, re-run on the new CLI — this one I added because it is the most consequential documented behaviour and precisely the kind Req 2 warns expires silently. At sprint 19's gate, on CLI 2.1.259, `node -e "require('fs').writeFileSync('<outside path>')"` ran with zero denials and the file landed outside the working directory. Re-run now on 2.1.261, with only `Bash(node *)` granted: zero denials, file written, contents "written". UNCHANGED.
   That independently corroborates the anchor message's own claim that "this bound has already survived one real CLI update unchanged" — I did not take that on the document's word, and it is true.

So the sample I re-ran is: one rejection rule, one OS-level protection, one allow/deny interaction, and one known escape. All four behave as documented, on 2.1.261.

================================================================
CRITERION — THE PERMISSION MODEL STILL BEHAVES AS DOCUMENTED: PASS
================================================================
The three named as "the three the grant is argued from" are entries 1, 2 and 3 above, all confirmed live. Nothing the grant's argument rests on has drifted on this CLI.

================================================================
CORRECTIONS TO MY OWN WORK, RECORDED RATHER THAN OMITTED
================================================================
1. AN UNINTENDED $0.93. My control invocation used `2>&1 >/dev/null | grep`, whose redirect order does not do what I intended — stdout went to the pipe rather than to /dev/null, and more importantly the run was a real, billed qa1 audit rather than the cheap check I meant it to be. The control result is still valid (no staleness warning at a matching version) but it cost about nine times what it should have. Recording it because it is the user's money and because a report that only mentions costs when they were deliberate is not an honest cost record.

2. I CHECKED THE WRONG PROFILE FIRST on the git push/status entry. I read `HEADLESS_PERMISSION_PROFILES.pipeman` and found `disallowedTools: []` with `Bash(git push *)` present in its ALLOW list — which looked like the documented behaviour was wrong, and is not. Pipeman's base profile is supposed to allow pushing; that is its job. The criterion's "the grant" means the owned-repository broad grant, whose OWNED_REPOSITORY_DISALLOWED_TOOLS is `["Bash(git push *)"]` subtracting one verb from a broad `Bash(git *)`. Corrected and then tested live. This is the fourth time across recent gates that I have probed a neighbouring surface before the right one; each was caught before it reached a verdict, but the pattern is mine and worth naming.

================================================================
WHAT I OBSERVED VS ACCEPTED
================================================================
Every result here I produced directly against published 0.1.22 and CLI 2.1.261. The staleness warning was produced by a stubbed version rather than by waiting for a real drift, which is the only way to observe it on demand; the control used my real CLI. The push denial was confirmed against the remote's refs, not the agent's summary. The anchor document's claim that the bound survived a CLI update was re-run rather than relayed.

Pipeman's request — that the warning fires on mismatch and stays non-blocking either way — is confirmed in both directions.

================================================================
RECOMMENDATION
================================================================
Ship-ready. The permission findings now carry the CLI version they were established against, drift is visible to whoever is about to rely on them, and the signal is a warning on stderr that neither blocks the run nor corrupts the headless stream. The four entries I independently re-ran all still hold on 2.1.261, including the escape that would have been the most damaging one to have expired quietly.

Nothing carries forward as a defect. The one thing worth saying about the design rather than the release: an anchor that equals the running version is the easy case, and the warning's value only shows the first time someone upgrades their CLI and reads it. That moment is now covered, which is the entire point of the sprint.

This PASS means the code is ready, not that anyone is authorized to close sprint 21.
